_comment: T-0072: Soviet brutalist/constructivist reference corpus for SDXL style LoRA. 13-asset-pipeline.md §3.2. Images are fetched by running: python -m lora_train.fetch --download. sha256 fields are null until fetched.

prefer: Exterior facades showing repetitive modular geometry (a brutalist facade is a tileset)
Flat or nearly flat camera angle — side-on or head-on, no strong perspective recede
Hard geometric silhouettes with minimal organic intrusion (trees, sky secondary)
Desaturated tonal range — concrete greys, oxide rust, institutional green, deep shadow
Decay and weathering visible — stains, spalling, watermarks read as texture not error
Institutional interiors: corridors, stairwells, mechanical rooms with consistent palette
Scale that communicates mass — the building overwhelming rather than the surrounding
avoid: Interiors of private apartments or residential spaces
Obvious commercial signage or brand logos (would train model to reproduce text)
Heavy organic elements where vegetation takes >50% of frame
Strong perspective distortion (fisheye, ultra-wide with barrel distortion)
Night photography or heavily artificial lighting that loses structural read
Post-Soviet renovation that adds incongruous cladding or colour
Tourist-posed shots where the human figure dominates the frame

refs.curation_notes: Narkomfin building (Ginzburg, 1930). Canonical Constructivist ribbon facade. Horizontal banding, pilotis, repetitive window grid. Directly relevant to side-on corridor geometry.
MGU main tower. Massive Soviet institutional geometry. Repetitive window grid across enormous facade. Useful for scale and repetition cues.
Khrushchyovka panel block (Cheremushki, Moscow). Flat prefabricated panel facade, extremely repetitive module. The brutalist tileset archetype.
Ministry of Highways, Tbilisi (Chkhenkeli, 1975). Famous brutalist cantilever cascade. Hard geometric silhouette, massive concrete, institutionally desaturated.
Soviet panel housing in Rusanivka, Kyiv. Water-adjacent context gives reflection of the repetitive facade — useful for value study of panel geometry.
ZIL Cultural Centre (Vesnin brothers, 1931). Constructivist. Projecting volumes, horizontal ribbon windows, strong geometry. Interior corridor logic.
Large-panel Brezhnev-era block, head-on view. Nearly orthographic, repetitive grid. Oxide staining at joints. Close match for wall tile generation target.
VDNKh Pavilion 26, Moscow. Soviet expo modernism. Flat concrete facade, geometric ornament as surface texture, muted palette. Good prop reference.
Ukrainian Institute of Scientific and Technical Expertise, Kyiv. Brutalist grid facade, very high window-to-wall ratio. Lattice silhouette useful for tileset transitions.
Government House, Minsk (Langbard, 1934). Early Soviet classicism shading into constructivism. Massive orthographic facade, institutional scale, near-monochrome in overcast.
BSU main building, Minsk. Soviet modernist slab. Repetitive bays, concrete fins as vertical rhythm, institutional green visible in window soffits.
Novosibirsk Opera House (1941). Massive dome and colonnaded perimeter. Concrete in overcast gives the tonal baseline for the brutalist grey range.
Palace of Culture, Lviv. Soviet neoclassicism with brutalist proportions. Stacked pilasters as vertical tilestrip. Good for wall-to-ceiling transition geometry.
Interior stairwell of a Soviet panel apartment block. Institutional green dado rail, bare concrete above, fluorescent-lit. Directly matches corridor art direction.
Khrushchyovka entrance lobby. Tiled floor, painted concrete walls, rusted mailboxes. Colour palette sample: cream, ochre, grey, rust — all within the home palette family.
Abandoned factory floor, Russia. Concrete columns at regular intervals, broken glass overhead, decay and light shafts. Models the abandoned-industrial atmosphere.
Zelenograd panel block. Seam-jointed precast panels in overcast light. Joint lines become implicit tile grid. Very clean head-on framing.
Moscow brutalist housing, mild oblique angle. Shows corner treatment and balcony rhythm. Useful for wall-floor transition silhouette reference.
Soviet sports institute, Moscow. Horizontal ribbon windows alternating with concrete spandrels. Highly regular module, good rhythm reference for repeating tile sets.
Research institute, Akademgorodok. Late-Soviet institutional modernism. Deep-set windows casting shadow grids on concrete spandrel. Strong value contrast.
Lazdynai, Vilnius — award-winning Soviet housing (1973). Terraced on hillside, standardised modules. Shows module stacking and silhouette variety from identical units.
Riga Academy of Sciences (Stalinist skyscraper, 1958). Stepped massing, repetitive window grids across large floorplate. Scale and mass reference.
Lasnamäe panel estates, Tallinn. Estonian late-Soviet housing. Identical slab blocks against overcast — shows the repetition-as-landscape effect.
Soviet housing, Yerevan. Tufa stone cladding on concrete frame — warm variant of the grey range, showing the oxide/stone notes in the palette.
Soviet-era housing in Almaty. Central Asian context adds dust and faded paint. Useful for the desaturated warm-grey end of the palette.
Soviet administrative building, Tashkent. Precast concrete with decorative screens — shows how surface ornament can be achieved within the geometry.
Nemiga-area panel blocks, Minsk. Row of identical slabs, very flat lighting. Nearly orthographic side elevation visible in foreground block — direct tilestrip reference.
Eiguliai estate, Kaunas. Lithuanian Soviet housing. Very plain rectangular panels with square window grid. High-contrast in raking autumn light — good for shadow study.
Darnytsia housing, Kyiv. 1970s-80s Kyiv panel estate. Road-level view shows wall-floor interface at scale, pedestrian-height reference.
Lenin Square, Volgograd. Stalinist neoclassical facades flanking a plaza. Colossal repeated archway rhythm, institutional ochre plaster over concrete — warm palette extreme.
Abandoned kolkhoz building, Russia. Collapsed roof sections, bare concrete, weed growth at margins. Heavy decay — good for weathering texture reference.
Close-up factory wall. Precast concrete panels with visible aggregate, rust runs from embedded iron, moss in joints. Material texture reference — best for LoRA surface learning.
Apartment facade, Pripyat. 40 years of abandonment — faded panel paint, vegetation beginning to reassert, structural bones still dominant. Canonical abandoned-Soviet reference.
Palace of Culture, Pripyat. Concrete modernist cultural building abandoned post-1986. Strong horizontal mass, stripped to essential geometry by abandonment.
ChNPP administration building. Nuclear-plant institutional modernism — exactly the visual register the game targets. Concrete, functional geometry, institutional scale.
Institutional corridor. Tiled lower walls (cream/green), painted upper section, fluorescent strip lighting, linoleum floor. The interior tileset material palette in one frame.
Exposed-concrete stairwell. Formwork-marked concrete, steel handrail, terrazzo floor edge. Good for the stairwell vertical-transition tile type.
Abandoned boiler room. Pipes, valves, concrete walls, rust and corrosion throughout. Industrial prop reference for the Signal Tower mechanical archetype.
GES-2 power station exterior (1907, renovated). Brick and concrete combined industrial heritage. Chimneys, geometric massing, industrial scale — good for exterior tile reference.
ZIL factory exterior wall. Pre-war Soviet industrial brick with later concrete additions. Weathered surface, geometric mass. Seam between different construction eras visible.
